addmaths-0606-lines-distance-midpoint-gr.description: Move between coordinates, lengths, midpoints and gradients without reversing one difference.

sections.title: How far apart are the two points?
sections.label: Length
sections.intro: Use Pythagoras with the horizontal and vertical displacements. When the length is known and a coordinate is missing, use the position of the point to select the correct sign.

blocks.html: Distance is \(\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\). A negative displacement still contributes a positive square.

figure.alt: A line segment, its midpoint and a rise–run triangle
figure.caption: The same direction is used for the horizontal and vertical differences.

blocks.prompt:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-11,1)\) and \(Q(-7,23)\).

Find the exact length of the baseline.
blocks.hint: Find the two coordinate differences before using Pythagoras. The exact length is the square root of their sum of squares.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal and vertical differences are \(4\) and \(22\), respectively. Hence \(PQ^2=4^2+22^2=16+484=500\).

\(PQ=\sqrt{100\times5}=10\sqrt5\).

blocks.html: Add the squared changes before taking a square root.

blocks.title: Choose the sign of the missing displacement
blocks.prompt: \(A(1,7)\) and \(B(9,r)\) are 17 units apart. \(B\) is below \(A\). Find \(r\).
blocks.hint: The horizontal displacement is \(8\). Find the magnitude of \(r-7\) using Pythagoras, then use the position of \(B\) to choose its sign.

retry.feedback: \(r=22\) is 17 units from \(A\), but it puts \(B\) above \(A\). Choose the negative vertical displacement.

blocks.prompt: Find the exact distance from \(A(-1,2)\) to \(B(3,10)\).
blocks.hint: The squared length is the sum of the squares of \(4\) and \(8\). Look for a square factor in this sum.

retry.feedback: Take the positive square root of the sum of squares to get the length.

blocks.html: Leave a surd in exact form unless the question asks for a rounded distance.

sections.title: How can I recover a missing endpoint?
sections.label: Midpoint
sections.intro: Write a separate average for x and for y. Read each equation backwards to recover the unknown coordinate.

blocks.html: For a segment with midpoint \(M\), its missing end is found by doubling each coordinate of \(M\) and subtracting the corresponding known coordinate.

blocks.prompt:
A segment has endpoint \(P(3,3)\) and midpoint \(M(5,-10)\).

Find the other endpoint.
blocks.hint: Let the other endpoint be \((u,v)\). Write one average for each coordinate.
blocks.solution:
The averages give \(\frac{3+u}{2}=5\) and \(\frac{3+v}{2}=-10\).

Therefore \(u=10-3=7\) and \(v=-20-3=-23\). The endpoint is \((7,-23)\).

blocks.html: Averaging x with y mixes the directions.

blocks.prompt: The midpoint of \(PQ\) is on the x-axis and has x-coordinate \(-1\). If \(P(2,3)\), find \(Q\).
blocks.hint: Write the midpoint as \((-1,0)\) and reverse the two coordinate averages separately.
blocks.solution:
The midpoint is \((-1,0)\). If \(Q=(u,v)\), then \(2+u=2(-1)=-2\) and \(3+v=0\).

Solving gives \(Q(-4,-3)\).

blocks.html: Substitute the recovered end into the original coordinate averages.

sections.title: How do I give a signed gradient?
sections.label: Gradient
sections.intro: Keep the same point order in both differences. A graph slopes upwards to the right when the gradient is positive.

blocks.html: Gradient is \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\). It is undefined when the horizontal change is zero.

blocks.prompt:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-2,6)\) and \(Q(2,38)\).

Find the gradient of the baseline.
blocks.hint: With horizontal difference \(2-(-2)\), the matching vertical difference is \(38-6\). Put the vertical difference in the numerator.
blocks.solution:
Use vertical change over horizontal change: \(\frac{32}{4}\).

\(8\)

blocks.html: A negative gradient can come from a positive horizontal change and a negative vertical change.

blocks.title: Recover the height from a negative gradient
blocks.prompt: From \(P(2,6)\) to \(Q(7,h)\) the gradient is \(-\frac35\). Find \(h\).
blocks.hint: Multiply the gradient by the signed horizontal change to find \(h-6\).
blocks.solution: The horizontal change is \(7-2=5\), so \(h-6=5\left(-\frac35\right)=-3\). Hence \(h=3\).

retry.feedback: The line slopes down as \(x\) increases. Use a vertical change of \(-3\).

blocks.prompt: Find the gradient of the line from \(P(-3,4)\) to \(Q(5,-2)\).
blocks.hint: Use \(Q-P\) in the numerator and denominator. The y-coordinate decreases as x increases.
blocks.solution:
The vertical change is \(-2-4=-6\) and the horizontal change is \(5-(-3)=8\).

Therefore the gradient is \(\frac{-6}{8}=-\frac34\).

retry.feedback: The line falls as you move to the right. Keep the minus sign from the change in y.

blocks.html: A negative gradient cannot be a negative length.

examples.title: Use a right triangle to find a length
examples.question: Find the exact length of the segment joining \(P(-2,1)\) and \(Q(4,5)\).
solution: Draw a horizontal step from \(P\) to \((4,1)\), then a vertical step up to \(Q\). The step lengths are \(4-(-2)=6\) and \(5-1=4\).
\(PQ\) is the hypotenuse, so \(PQ^2=6^2+4^2=36+16=52\).
Use the non-negative square root for a length. \(PQ=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}\).

examples.title: Recover a coordinate from a given distance
examples.question: \(P(-2,1)\) and \(Q(4,k)\) are 10 units apart. \(Q\) is above \(P\). Find \(k\).
solution: The horizontal change from \(P\) to \(Q\) is \(4-(-2)=6\), and the signed vertical change is \(k-1\).
Use Pythagoras with the given length. \(6^2+(k-1)^2=10^2\), so \((k-1)^2=64\).
The displacement could be \(8\) or \(-8\) from the equation alone. Above \(P\) gives \(k-1=8\), so \(k=9\).

examples.title: Recover the other end of a segment
examples.question: One endpoint of a segment is \(P(3,-1)\). Its midpoint is \(M(1,2)\). Find the other endpoint \(Q\).
solution: Let \(Q=(u,v)\). The x-coordinates average to \(1\), so \(\frac{3+u}{2}=1\). Hence \(u=2-3=-1\).
The y-coordinates average to \(2\), so \(\frac{-1+v}{2}=2\). Hence \(v=4+1=5\).
The other endpoint is \(Q(-1,5)\). The same move, 2 left and 3 up, takes you from \(P\) to \(M\) and from \(M\) to \(Q\).

examples.title: Use a shared midpoint to locate a vertex
examples.question: The diagonals of a parallelogram are \(AC\) and \(BD\). The vertices are \(A(-2,0)\), \(C(6,4)\) and \(B(0,5)\). Find \(D\).
solution: The diagonals bisect each other. The midpoint of \(AC\) is \(\left(\frac{-2+6}{2},\frac{0+4}{2}\right)=(2,2)\).
From \(B(0,5)\) to the midpoint, move 2 right and 3 down. Repeat that same move from the midpoint to \(D\).
\(D=(4,-1)\). The average of \(B\) and \(D\) gives \((2,2)\), as required.

examples.title: Compare the steepness of two ramps
examples.question: Ramp \(A\) runs from \((1,2)\) to \((7,5)\). Ramp \(B\) runs from \((0,1)\) to \((8,7)\). Which ramp is steeper?
solution: For ramp \(A\), the rise is \(5-2=3\) and the run is \(7-1=6\). Its gradient is \(\frac36=\frac12\).
For ramp \(B\), the gradient is \(\frac{7-1}{8-0}=\frac68=\frac34\).
Both ramps rise as x increases. Ramp \(B\) is steeper because \(\frac34>\frac12\). Compare the rise per unit of run.

examples.title: Use a negative fractional gradient backwards
examples.question: A line joins \(A(-2,5)\) to \(B(4,t)\). Its gradient is \(-\frac23\). Find \(t\).
solution: Moving from \(A\) to \(B\) gives a horizontal displacement of \(6\). Write \(\frac{t-5}{6}=-\frac23\).
The vertical displacement is \(-4\). Therefore \(t=5-4=1\).
A negative gradient means the point farther right is lower. That agrees with \(1<5\).

extraPractice.prompt: The endpoints of a segment are \(A(7,4)\) and \(B(3,1)\). Find its length.
extraPractice.hint: From \(A\) to \(B\) the displacements are negative. Their squares are positive.

extraPractice.prompt: Find how many units longer \(AB\) is than \(AC\), given \(A(1,1)\), \(B(7,9)\) and \(C(5,1)\).
extraPractice.hint: Calculate both lengths first. The segment \(AC\) is horizontal.
extraPractice.solution:
\(AB=\sqrt{(7-1)^2+(9-1)^2}=\sqrt{36+64}=10\).

The points \(A\) and \(C\) have the same y-coordinate, so \(AC=5-1=4\). The difference is \(10-4=6\).

extraPractice.prompt:
A segment has endpoint \(P(-8,4)\) and midpoint \(M(-6,-10)\).

Find the other endpoint.
extraPractice.hint: Use each midpoint equation in reverse.
extraPractice.solution:
Double the midpoint coordinate and subtract the known endpoint: \(Q=(-6,-10)\times2-(-8,4)\).

\((-4,-24)\)

extraPractice.prompt: Find the midpoint of \(A(-3,5)\) and \(B(4,-1)\).
extraPractice.hint: Average the two x-coordinates and the two y-coordinates separately. A midpoint need not have integer coordinates.
extraPractice.solution: \(M=\left(\frac{-3+4}{2},\frac{5-1}{2}\right)=\left(\frac12,2\right)\).

extraPractice.prompt: Find the gradient of the line through \((-5,3)\) and \((2,3)\).
extraPractice.hint: Compare the y-coordinates first. A horizontal line has no vertical change.
extraPractice.solution: \(m=\frac{3-3}{2-(-5)}=\frac07=0\). The denominator is non-zero because the x-coordinates differ.

extraPractice.prompt: A line with gradient \(\frac32\) passes through \(A(1,-2)\) and \(B(q,7)\). Find \(q\).
extraPractice.hint: A rise of \(9\) is three times the rise in a step with rise 3 and run 2.
extraPractice.solution:
The vertical change is \(7-(-2)=9\). Write \(\frac9{q-1}=\frac32\).

\(18=3(q-1)\) gives \(q-1=6\), so \(q=7\).

addmaths-0606-lines-parallel-perpendicul.description: Use direction conditions to find lines and missing coordinates.

sections.title: What do parallel lines have in common?
sections.label: Parallel
sections.intro: Horizontal progress of one unit produces the same vertical change on parallel lines.

blocks.html: Parallel non-vertical lines have equal gradients. If the vertical intercepts are equal as well, both equations describe the same line. Two vertical lines \(x=a\) and \(x=b\) are distinct and parallel when \(a\ne b\).

blocks.prompt:
The line \(L\) has equation \(3x+11y=1\). A line \(K\) passes through \(P(11,13)\) and is parallel to \(L\).

Find the gradient of \(K\).
blocks.hint: Move \(3x\) to the right of the equals sign before dividing by \(11\).
blocks.solution:
Rearrange the given equation to obtain \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+\frac{1}{11}\). Parallel lines have equal gradients.

\(-\frac{3}{11}\)

blocks.html: A common gradient and intercept describe the same line.

blocks.title: Pick a distinct parallel line
blocks.prompt: Which line is parallel to \(6x+9y=12\) and distinct from it?
blocks.hint: First divide the original equation by 3. Compare the coefficients on the left and the constant on the right.
blocks.solution: The original is \(2x+3y=4\). Changing its right-hand side to 7 changes the intercept while keeping the slope, so \(2x+3y=7\) is distinct and parallel.

retry.feedback: \(2x+3y=4\) is exactly the original equation after division by 3. The question asks for a different line.

blocks.prompt: A line is parallel to \(4x-3y=6\). Find its gradient.
blocks.hint: Move \(4x\) away from the y-term, then divide every term by \(-3\).
blocks.solution: \(-3y=6-4x\) gives \(y=\frac43x-2\). Parallel lines share the gradient \(\frac43\).

blocks.html: Rearrange the given equation for y before reading the gradient.

sections.title: Which gradient gives a right angle?
sections.label: Perpendicular
sections.intro: Switch rise and run, then change one sign. This makes the gradient the negative reciprocal.

blocks.html: Non-vertical perpendicular lines have gradient product \(-1\). A horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.

figure.alt: A segment AB and its perpendicular bisector meeting at M
figure.caption: The lines meet at a right angle at the midpoint M.

blocks.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(0,-12)\) to \(B(4,18)\). The line \(K\) is perpendicular to \(AB\) and passes through \(P(22,-8)\).

Find an equation of \(K\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
blocks.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(\frac{15}{2}\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{2}{15}\).

Substitute \((22,-8)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=-\frac{76}{15}\).

\(y=-\frac{2}{15}x-\frac{76}{15}\)

blocks.html: Negating without taking the reciprocal normally produces the wrong angle.

blocks.prompt: Find the equation of the line through \((2,3)\) perpendicular to \(2x+3y=12\).
blocks.hint: The given slope is negative. What positive slope will make the product equal to \(-1\)?
blocks.solution:
Rearranging gives \(y=-\frac23x+4\). The perpendicular gradient is \(\frac32\).

Substituting into \(y=\frac32x+c\) gives \(3=3+c\), so \(c=0\). The equation is \(y=\frac32x\).

blocks.html: Test a horizontal or vertical line separately before using a reciprocal.

sections.title: Where does a perpendicular bisector pass?
sections.label: Bisector
sections.intro: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint and makes a right angle with the segment. For a horizontal or vertical segment, choose the other axis direction directly.

blocks.html: A point lies on a perpendicular bisector precisely when it is the same distance from the two ends.

blocks.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(-5,-15)\) to \(B(-1,21)\). Its midfield boundary is the perpendicular bisector.

Find an equation of the perpendicular bisector.
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
blocks.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(9\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{1}{9}\).

The midpoint is \((-3,3)\). Substitute \((-3,3)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=\frac{8}{3}\).

\(y=-\frac{1}{9}x+\frac{8}{3}\)

blocks.html: The perpendicular through an endpoint is a different line.

blocks.title: Bisect a vertical segment
blocks.prompt: Find an equation of the perpendicular bisector of \(A(-2,-5)\) and \(B(-2,3)\).
blocks.hint: The x-coordinates are equal, so \(AB\) is vertical. Through its midpoint draw a horizontal line.
blocks.solution: The midpoint is \((-2,-1)\). The perpendicular direction is horizontal, giving \(y=-1\).

retry.feedback: \(x=-2\) is the line containing \(AB\). The bisector must be perpendicular, so use a constant y-coordinate.

blocks.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(A(-4,0)\) and \(B(2,-4)\).
blocks.hint: Average the endpoints, then take the negative reciprocal of the segment gradient.
blocks.solution:
The midpoint is \((-1,-2)\). The segment gradient is \(\frac{-4-0}{2-(-4)}=-\frac23\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(\frac32\).

Use \(y+2=\frac32(x+1)\). Expanding gives \(y=\frac32x-\frac12\).

blocks.html: Find the midpoint and gradient in separate lines of working.

examples.title: Find a parallel line through a point
examples.question: The line \(K\) passes through \((6,1)\) and is parallel to \(2x+3y=9\). Find an equation of \(K\).
solution: Rearrange the given equation to give \(3y=-2x+9\), so \(y=-\frac23x+3\). The gradient of both lines is \(-\frac23\).
Substitute \((6,1)\) into \(y=-\frac23x+c\). Then \(1=-4+c\), giving \(c=5\).
Therefore \(K\) is \(y=-\frac23x+5\). When \(x=6\), the new equation gives \(y=1\).

examples.title: Distinguish parallel lines from the same line
examples.question: Compare \(L:2x-3y=6\), \(M:4x-6y=12\) and \(N:4x-6y=9\). Which describe the same line, and which are distinct parallel lines?
solution: Divide every term of \(M\) by 2. The result is \(2x-3y=6\), so \(L\) and \(M\) are the same line.
Divide every term of \(N\) by 2. Its equation becomes \(2x-3y=\frac92\). It has the same gradient as \(L\) and a different vertical intercept.
\(N\) is therefore distinct from and parallel to both \(L\) and \(M\).

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular through an off-line point
examples.question: Find an equation of the line through \(P(6,2)\) that is perpendicular to the line from \(A(-1,0)\) to \(B(3,6)\).
solution: The gradient from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(\frac{6-0}{3-(-1)}=\frac64=\frac32\).
Take the negative reciprocal to get \(-\frac23\). The product \(\frac32\times\left(-\frac23\right)=-1\) checks the right angle.
Use \(y-2=-\frac23(x-6)\). Expand and add \(2\) to obtain \(y=-\frac23x+6\).

examples.title: Choose the perpendicular from standard form
examples.question: Which of \(3x+2y=5\), \(2x+3y=5\) and \(2x-3y=5\) is perpendicular to \(3x-2y=8\)?
solution: Isolate \(y\) in the given equation. \(2y=3x-8\), so its gradient is \(\frac32\).
The perpendicular gradient must be \(-\frac23\). The three candidates have gradients \(-\frac32\), \(-\frac23\) and \(\frac23\), respectively.
Therefore \(2x+3y=5\) is perpendicular. Changing only the sign of the original gradient would give \(-\frac32\), which does not give a product of \(-1\).

examples.title: Find and test a perpendicular bisector
examples.question: Find the perpendicular bisector of \(A(0,1)\) and \(B(6,5)\). Check that \((5,0)\) lies on it.
solution: The midpoint is \(M(3,3)\) by averaging each pair of coordinates. The segment gradient is \(\frac{5-1}{6-0}=\frac23\).
The perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac32\). The line through \(M\) is \(y-3=-\frac32(x-3)\), which gives \(3x+2y=15\).
At \((5,0)\), \(3(5)+2(0)=15\), so the point lies on the bisector. Its squared distances to the ends are \(5^2+(-1)^2=26\) and \((-1)^2+(-5)^2=26\).

examples.title: Bisect a horizontal segment
examples.question: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of \(A(-4,2)\) and \(B(6,2)\).
solution: The midpoint has x-coordinate \(\frac{-4+6}{2}=1\), and its y-coordinate is \(2\).
The segment is horizontal. Its perpendicular bisector must be vertical through \((1,2)\).
A vertical line has a fixed x-coordinate. Its equation is \(x=1\).

extraPractice.prompt: A line through \((5,-2)\) is parallel to \(x=-1\). Find its equation.
extraPractice.hint: Every point of \(x=-1\) has the same x-coordinate. A parallel line also has a fixed x-coordinate.
extraPractice.solution: The line \(x=-1\) is vertical. A vertical line through \((5,-2)\) has equation \(x=5\).

extraPractice.prompt: The lines \(6x+4y=8\) and \(kx-2y=1\) are parallel. Find \(k\).
extraPractice.hint: Rearrange both equations to read their gradients. In the second line the gradient is \(\frac{k}{2}\).
extraPractice.solution:
The first gradient is \(-\frac64=-\frac32\). The second equation gives \(y=\frac{k}{2}x-\frac12\).

Equating the gradients gives \(\frac{k}{2}=-\frac32\), so \(k=-3\).

extraPractice.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(8,-12)\) to \(B(12,18)\). The line \(K\) is perpendicular to \(AB\) and passes through \(P(30,-16)\).

Find an equation of \(K\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
extraPractice.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(\frac{15}{2}\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{2}{15}\).

Substitute \((30,-16)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=-12\).

\(y=-\frac{2}{15}x-12\)

extraPractice.prompt: Find the equation of the line through \((3,-4)\) that is perpendicular to \(x=8\).
extraPractice.hint: Identify the direction of \(x=8\) before using a gradient rule.
extraPractice.solution: \(x=8\) is vertical, so a perpendicular is horizontal. Every point has the y-coordinate \(-4\), giving \(y=-4\).

extraPractice.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(3,-15)\) to \(B(7,21)\). Its midfield boundary is the perpendicular bisector.

Find an equation of the perpendicular bisector.
extraPractice.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
extraPractice.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(9\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{1}{9}\).

The midpoint is \((5,3)\). Substitute \((5,3)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=\frac{32}{9}\).

\(y=-\frac{1}{9}x+\frac{32}{9}\)

extraPractice.prompt: A line is the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\), where \(A(-2,7)\) and \(B(8,7)\). Give its equation.
extraPractice.hint: The segment is horizontal. The bisector is vertical through the midpoint.
extraPractice.solution: The x-coordinate of the midpoint is \(\frac{-2+8}{2}=3\). The vertical line through the midpoint is \(x=3\).

glossary.definition: Two distinct straight lines with the same direction.
A line that divides a segment into two equal lengths.

revision.body:
What do parallel lines have in common?

Distinct non-vertical parallel lines have equal gradients and different vertical intercepts. Equal gradients and equal intercepts describe the same line.

Which gradient gives a right angle?

If both gradients are defined, perpendicular lines have gradient product \(-1\). A horizontal and a vertical line are also perpendicular.

Where does a perpendicular bisector pass?

Find the midpoint and give the perpendicular equation through it. Replace a horizontal direction with a vertical one, or a vertical direction with a horizontal one.

sections.title: How does a point fix the position of a line?
sections.label: Equation
sections.intro: A gradient fixes the direction. Find it from two points if needed. Use \(y=mx+c\) when the intercept is useful, or start with \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\) when a point and a slope are already given.

blocks.html: Either use \(y=mx+c\) and solve for \(c\), or write \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\).

blocks.prompt:
A path passes through \(A(-7,17)\) and \(B(-3,25)\). A second path lies on \(11x+y=-34\).

Find the equation of the first line.
blocks.hint: Substitute a known point into the line with the correct gradient.
blocks.solution:
Use gradient \(2\) and substitute \((-7,17)\) for a point on the line.

\(y=2x+31\)

blocks.html: The y-coordinate of the given point is its intercept only if its x-coordinate is zero.

blocks.prompt: Find the equation of the line through \((2,-3)\) and \((-4,6)\).
blocks.hint: Find the gradient first. Use \((2,-3)\) to calculate the intercept, even if it might be zero.

blocks.html: Check the final equation with both given points when possible.

sections.title: Where do two lines meet?
sections.label: Meeting
sections.intro: At an intersection one pair of coordinates satisfies both equations. Equate two expressions for \(y\), or substitute directly when one equation fixes a coordinate.

blocks.html: If both equations give \(y\), set their right-hand sides equal, then substitute the resulting x-coordinate back.

figure.alt: Two straight lines cross at a marked point
figure.caption: The point of intersection satisfies both equations.

blocks.prompt:
A motion sensor gives the position \(y=2x+47\). A second sensor gives \(14x+y=-113\).

Find the point where the lines cross.
blocks.hint: Solve the equations simultaneously and then substitute.
blocks.solution:
The second line is \(y=-14x-113\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.

Rearranging gives \(16x=-160\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=27\).

\((-10,27)\)

blocks.html: The x-coordinate alone does not describe the intersection.

blocks.prompt: Find the intersection of \(y=3x+1\) and \(y=1-2x\).
blocks.hint: Set the two right-hand sides equal. Both equations show the same intercept.
blocks.solution:
\(3x+1=1-2x\) gives \(5x=0\), hence \(x=0\).

Substitution into either equation gives \(y=1\), so the intersection is \((0,1)\).

blocks.html: Use the simpler equation to find y, then verify the pair in the other equation.

sections.title: When is standard form useful?
sections.label: Standard form
sections.intro: If the same variable has opposite coefficients, add the equations to eliminate it. If the coefficients match, subtract instead. Substitute back to find the second coordinate.

blocks.html: Keep equations in standard form when it makes elimination simpler. You may multiply every term of an equation by the same non-zero number to match coefficients.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(3x+2y=11\) and \(x+2y=7\) simultaneously. Give the point of intersection.
blocks.hint: Both equations have \(+2y\). Subtract the second equation from the first.
blocks.solution:
Subtract to get \(2x=4\), so \(x=2\).

Then \(2+2y=7\) gives \(y=\frac52\). The first equation checks: \(3(2)+2\left(\frac52\right)=11\).

blocks.html: The sign of the x-coefficient changes when you move the x-term to the other side.

blocks.title: Check an intersection in both equations
blocks.prompt: Find the exact intersection of \(2x+3y=16\) and \(4x-3y=5\).
blocks.hint: Add the equations to eliminate \(y\). Substitute the result for \(x\) into either equation to find \(y\).
blocks.solution:
Adding gives \(6x=21\), so \(x=\frac72\). Then \(7+3y=16\), which gives \(y=3\).

The intersection is \(\left(\frac72,3\right)\). Check that \(4\left(\frac72\right)-3(3)=5\).

retry.feedback: The coordinates are reversed. The equation \(6x=21\) gives the first coordinate.

blocks.prompt: Find the intersection of \(2x+3y=7\) and \(x-y=1\).
blocks.hint: Multiply the second equation by 3, including the term on the right. Its y-term will cancel the first equation's.
blocks.solution:
Multiply to get \(3x-3y=3\). Adding to \(2x+3y=7\) gives \(5x=10\).

With \(x=2\), \(2-y=1\) gives \(y=1\). The two lines meet at \((2,1)\).

blocks.html: Use exact fractions or clear denominators across the whole equation.

examples.title: Find a line from two points
examples.question: Find the equation of the line through \(A(-1,4)\) and \(B(3,2)\). Give your answer in the form \(y=mx+c\).
solution: The gradient is \(\frac{2-4}{3-(-1)}=-\frac12\). Start with \(y=-\frac12x+c\).
Substitute \(A(-1,4)\) to get \(4=\frac12+c\), so \(c=\frac72\).
Therefore \(y=-\frac12x+\frac72\). The line also gives \(y=2\) when \(x=3\).

examples.title: Use a point and a known gradient
examples.question: A line passes through \((2,-3)\) and has gradient \(\frac32\). Find where it meets the y-axis.
solution: Write \(y-(-3)=\frac32(x-2)\), which is \(y+3=\frac32x-3\).
Subtract \(3\) to get \(y=\frac32x-6\). The y-axis has \(x=0\), which gives \(y=-6\).
The intercept is \((0,-6)\). From the intercept, a horizontal change of \(2\) gives a vertical change of \(3\), reaching the given point.

examples.title: Equate two expressions for the same y-coordinate
examples.question: Find the point where \(y=2x-5\) and \(y=7-x\) intersect.
solution: At the meeting point both values of \(y\) agree. Hence \(2x-5=7-x\).
Add \(x\) and \(5\) to both sides to obtain \(3x=12\), so \(x=4\).
Substitute back. The first equation gives \(y=2(4)-5=3\), and the second gives \(7-4=3\), so the intersection is \((4,3)\).

examples.title: Use a vertical line to fix the input
examples.question: Find the point where the line \(x=-2\) meets \(3x-2y=4\).
solution: Every point on the vertical line has x-coordinate \(-2\). Substitute that value into the other line.
\(3(-2)-2y=4\) gives \(-2y=10\). Dividing both sides by \(-2\) gives \(y=-5\).
The intersection is \((-2,-5)\). The equation \(x=-2\) supplies one coordinate directly.

examples.title: Match coefficients before subtracting
examples.question: Find the intersection of \(2x+3y=16\) and \(x+y=6\).
solution: Double every term of \(x+y=6\) to get \(2x+2y=12\). The coefficients of \(x\) now agree.
Subtract this equation from the first. \((2x+3y)-(2x+2y)=16-12\), so \(y=4\).
Then \(x=6-4=2\). The point \((2,4)\) gives \(2(2)+3(4)=16\) in the first equation.

examples.title: Eliminate a variable without fractions
examples.question: Find the intersection of \(3x+2y=5\) and \(5x-2y=11\).
solution: Add the equations. The y-terms cancel, leaving \(8x=16\), so \(x=2\).
Substitute into \(3x+2y=5\). Then \(6+2y=5\), which gives \(y=-\frac12\).
The intersection is \(\left(2,-\frac12\right)\). The second line gives \(5(2)-2\left(-\frac12\right)=11\).

sections.title: How do intercepts give a triangle's area?
sections.label: Intercepts
sections.intro: The axes meet at right angles. Find their intersections with the third side to identify the base and height.

blocks.html: An x-intercept has \(y=0\) and a y-intercept has \(x=0\). Use their positive distances from the origin in the area formula.

figure.alt: A line and the coordinate axes enclose a right triangle
figure.caption: The intercepts give the base and perpendicular height.

blocks.prompt:
The line \(25x+4y=100\) and the positive coordinate axes enclose a triangle.

Give the point where the line meets the x-axis.
blocks.hint: Use y = 0.

blocks.html: Find the two intercepts by setting a different coordinate to zero each time.

blocks.prompt: The line \(3x+2y=-12\) forms a triangle with the coordinate axes. Find the area of the triangle.
blocks.hint: Find both intercepts, then use their positive distances from the origin.
blocks.solution:
Set \(y=0\) to get \(x=-4\). Set \(x=0\) to get \(y=-6\).

The right-angled sides have lengths \(4\) and \(6\). Area \(=\frac12(4)(6)=12\).

blocks.html: A negative intercept can still give a positive length.

sections.title: How do I measure the perpendicular height?
sections.label: Heights
sections.intro: For a vertical base, use a horizontal distance for the height. For a horizontal base, use a vertical distance. Measure to the line through the base, extending it if necessary.

blocks.html: If the base is on \(x=c\), its perpendicular height from \((u,v)\) is \(|u-c|\). If the base is on \(y=c\), the height is \(|v-c|\).

blocks.prompt:
A site plan forms a triangle with vertices \(A(4,10)\), \(B(4,12)\) and \(C(19,9)\).

Find the perpendicular distance from \(C\) to the line \(AB\).
blocks.hint: Use the difference of x-coordinates.
blocks.solution:
The line \(AB\) is vertical, so its perpendicular distance is the horizontal difference.

\(15\)

blocks.html: A sloping side does not normally give the perpendicular height.

blocks.title: Measure the height to the base line
blocks.prompt: A triangle has vertices \(A(-1,3)\), \(B(7,3)\) and \(C(9,-2)\). Using \(AB\) as the base, find its area in square units.
blocks.hint: The base is horizontal and its line is \(y=3\). Use the difference between \(3\) and \(-2\) for the height.
blocks.solution: The base is \(7-(-1)=8\) and the perpendicular height is \(3-(-2)=5\). The area is \(\frac12\times8\times5=20\) square units.

retry.feedback: The product \(8\times5\) gives the area of a corresponding rectangle. Take half for the triangle.

blocks.prompt: Triangle \(ABC\) has \(A(-1,2)\), \(B(-1,9)\) and \(C(-6,3)\). Use \(AB\) as the base to find the area.
blocks.hint: The base is vertical. Measure the height horizontally from \(x=-6\) to \(x=-1\).
blocks.solution:
\(AB=9-2=7\) and the perpendicular distance from \(C\) is \(|-6-(-1)|=5\).

The area is \(\frac12(7)(5)=\frac{35}{2}\).

blocks.html: Sketch the base and draw a small perpendicular mark beside the height.

sections.title: How can one diagonal simplify an outline?
sections.label: Split
sections.intro: Choose a diagonal that is horizontal or vertical. It gives both smaller triangles a convenient common base.

blocks.html: Each triangle contributes \(\frac{1}{2}bh\). With a common base, compare their areas by comparing their heights.

blocks.prompt:
A quadrilateral has vertices \(A(-1,13)\), \(C(17,12)\), \(B(-1,15)\) and \(D(-20,17)\) in that order.

Find the area of the quadrilateral.
blocks.hint: Add the two areas built on AB.
blocks.solution:
Draw diagonal \(AB\). The horizontal heights on its two sides are \(18\) and \(19\).

The total is \(\frac{1}{2}\times2\times37=37\).

\(37\) square units.

blocks.html: Check whether the two heights run to opposite sides of the line before adding the regions.

blocks.title: Recover a coordinate from a quadrilateral's area
blocks.prompt: A quadrilateral has consecutive vertices \(A(2,-2)\), \(C(5,1)\), \(B(2,4)\) and \(D(d,1)\) with \(d<2\). Its area is 24 square units. Find \(d\).
blocks.hint: Split at the vertical diagonal \(AB\). The height on the left is \(2-d\), measured from \(x=2\).
blocks.solution: The common base has length \(6\). The right and left heights are \(3\) and \(2-d\), so \(24=3(3+2-d)\). This gives \(d=-3\).

blocks.prompt: Two triangles share the base from \((1,2)\) to \((9,2)\). Their third vertices are \((4,5)\) and \((7,-3)\). Find their total area.
blocks.hint: The common base is horizontal. Calculate each height by comparing its y-coordinate with \(2\).
blocks.solution:
The base has length \(8\), with heights \(5-2=3\) and \(2-(-3)=5\).

The total area is \(\frac12(8)(3+5)=32\).

examples.title: Find the area bounded by a line and the axes
examples.question: Find the area of the triangle enclosed by \(2x+3y=12\) and the coordinate axes.
solution: On the x-axis \(y=0\), so \(2x=12\) and the intercept is \((6,0)\).
On the y-axis \(x=0\), so \(3y=12\) and the intercept is \((0,4)\).
The axes are perpendicular, giving a base of \(6\) and a height of \(4\). The area is \(\frac12\times6\times4=12\) square units.

examples.title: Use a negative intercept as a positive length
examples.question: The line \(x-2y=-8\) meets the coordinate axes. Find the area of the triangle formed with the origin.
solution: Set \(y=0\) to get \(x=-8\), so the x-intercept is \((-8,0)\). Set \(x=0\) to get \(-2y=-8\), so the y-intercept is \((0,4)\).
The horizontal side runs from \(-8\) to \(0\) and has length \(8\). The vertical side has length \(4\).
The area is \(\frac12\times8\times4=16\) square units. The sign of the x-intercept tells you which side of the origin to draw.

examples.title: Use the horizontal distance to a vertical side
examples.question: Find the area of the triangle with vertices \(A(2,1)\), \(B(2,7)\) and \(C(-3,4)\), using \(AB\) as the base.
solution: The base is vertical on \(x=2\), with length \(7-1=6\). A perpendicular to this base must be horizontal.
The perpendicular from \(C\) reaches the base at \((2,4)\). Its length is \(2-(-3)=5\).
The area is \(\frac12\times6\times5=15\) square units.

examples.title: Use the extension of a horizontal base
examples.question: A triangle has vertices \(A(-3,4)\), \(B(5,4)\) and \(C(8,-2)\). Find its area, using \(AB\) as the base.
solution: Both endpoints of \(AB\) have \(y=4\), so the base is horizontal and has length \(5-(-3)=8\).
The perpendicular from \(C\) meets the extension of \(AB\) at \(H(8,4)\). The height is \(4-(-2)=6\).
The area is \(\frac12\times8\times6=24\) square units.

examples.title: Use one diagonal as a common base
examples.question: The vertices of a quadrilateral in order are \(A(0,2)\), \(C(3,5)\), \(B(6,2)\) and \(D(1,-2)\). Find its area and the ratio of the areas of \(ACB\) and \(ADB\).
solution: The diagonal \(AB\) is horizontal on \(y=2\), of length \(6\). The vertices \(C\) and \(D\) lie on opposite sides of it.
Their perpendicular heights are \(5-2=3\) and \(2-(-2)=4\), giving triangle areas \(\frac12(6)(3)=9\) and \(\frac12(6)(4)=12\).
The total area is \(21\) square units. The area ratio is \(9:12=3:4\), which equals the ratio of heights because the base is shared.

examples.title: Use a known area to recover a vertex
examples.question: A quadrilateral has consecutive vertices \(A(0,0)\), \(C(6,2)\), \(B(0,4)\) and \(D(d,2)\), where \(d<0\). Its area is 22 square units. Find \(d\).
solution: The diagonal \(AB\) has length \(4\). The triangles on either side have perpendicular heights \(6\) and \(-d\).
Add the two areas to obtain \(22=\frac12(4)(6-d)=2(6-d)\).
This gives \(d=-5\). The heights are then \(6\) and \(5\), giving areas \(12\) and \(10\).

From a point \((u,v)\), the distance to a vertical base line \(x=c\) is \(|u-c|\). The distance to a horizontal base line \(y=c\) is \(|v-c|\).

How can one diagonal simplify an outline?

Each triangle contributes \(\frac{1}{2}bh\). When the diagonal separates the two triangles, use it as their common base and add their two areas.

addmaths-0606-lines-make-model-linear.description: Choose transformed axes and interpret the gradient and intercept.

sections.title: Which operations make a straight-line pattern?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: Undo the outer function first. Then look for one expression of x with a constant multiple and a constant term.

blocks.html: In \(\sqrt y=a+b/x\), the two axis variables can be \(Y=\sqrt y\) and \(X=1/x\). The relation then has the form \(Y=bX+a\).

blocks.prompt:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=\left(17+\frac{13}{x}\right)^3\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) on the horizontal axis.

Which expression should go on the vertical axis?
blocks.hint: Undo the outside operation to get a linear expression in X.
blocks.solution:
Take the positive cube root, then use \(X=\frac{1}{x}\).

That gives \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\) and \(Y=13X+17\).

\(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\)

blocks.html: The heading ‘Y against X’ puts Y on the vertical axis.

blocks.prompt: For \(x>2\), let \(y=\sqrt{4-\frac8x}\). Find the gradient of the straight graph with axes \(X=\frac1x\) and \(Y=y^2\).
blocks.hint: Square the original equation, then identify the coefficient of \(X\).
blocks.solution: \(Y=4-8X\), so the gradient is \(-8\). The constant \(4\) gives the vertical intercept of the line.

blocks.html: Write the two axis definitions before giving the gradient or intercept.

sections.title: How can a power model give a straight line?
sections.label: Power
sections.intro: A logarithm turns powers into multipliers and products into sums.

blocks.html: For \(y=Ax^n\), plot \(\log y\) against \(\log x\). The gradient is \(n\) and the intercept is \(\log A\).

figure.alt: Three points on a straight line in transformed coordinates
figure.caption: The horizontal axis is X, the chosen expression in x. The vertical axis is Y, the chosen expression in y.

blocks.prompt:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=2^{12}x^{16}\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=\log_2 x\) on the horizontal axis.

Which expression should go on the vertical axis?
blocks.hint: Use base 2 for both logarithms so that the transformed horizontal coordinate is \(\log_2 x\).
blocks.solution:
Use the product and power laws to convert \(\log_2(Ax^n)\) to \(\log_2 A+n\log_2 x\).

That gives \(Y=\log_2 y\) and \(Y=16X+12\).

\(Y=\log_2 y\)

blocks.html: The intercept is a logarithm of A. Undo it to find A itself.

blocks.title: Read the slope and intercept of a power model
blocks.prompt: Let \(y=9\sqrt{x}\) for \(x>0\). The axes are \(X=\log_3x\) and \(Y=\log_3y\). Give the gradient and the vertical intercept.
blocks.hint: Take \(\log_3\) of both sides and use the product and power laws.
blocks.solution: \(\log_3 y=\log_3 9+\frac12\log_3 x=2+\frac12X\). The gradient is \(\frac12\) and the intercept is \(2\).

retry.feedback: The exponent of \(x\) multiplies \(\log_3 x\), so copy that exponent into the coefficient of \(X\).
The intercept belongs to the transformed axis \(Y=\log_3 y\). Apply \(\log_3\) to the coefficient \(9\).

blocks.prompt: The model is \(y=27x^{-2}\) for \(x>0\). Find the vertical intercept as a number on the plot of \(Y=\log_3 y\) against \(X=\log_3x\).
blocks.hint: Use the product and power laws. The constant is \(\log_3 27\).
blocks.solution:
\(\log_3 y=\log_3 27-2\log_3x\). Since \(3^3=27\), this gives \(Y=3-2X\).

The value of \(Y\) at \(X=0\) is \(3\).

blocks.html: Use the same base for the logarithms on both axes.

sections.title: How does a logarithm undo an exponential model?
sections.label: Exponential
sections.intro: Taking natural logs undoes an outer exponential. If the base differs from \(e\), use the power law to bring its exponent in front of the logarithm.

blocks.html: If \(y=e^{ax^2+b}\), use \(Y=\ln y\) and \(X=x^2\). In \(Y=aX+b\), identify the constants by their roles.

blocks.prompt:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=e^{2x^2+6}\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=x^2\) on the horizontal axis.

Which expression should go on the vertical axis?
blocks.hint: Apply the inverse of \(e^u\) to recover the whole exponent \(2x^2+6\).
blocks.solution:
Taking natural logs removes the exponential. Put \(X=x^2\) for its quadratic input.

That gives \(Y=\ln y\) and \(Y=2X+6\).

\(Y=\ln y\)

blocks.html: Choose a horizontal variable that accounts for the power of x in the exponent.

blocks.prompt: The model is \(y=e^{5-3x^2}\). Find the gradient on the plot of \(\ln y\) against \(x^2\).
blocks.hint: Take natural logs and read the coefficient of \(x^2\).
blocks.solution: \(\ln y=5-3x^2\). For \(X=x^2\) and \(Y=\ln y\), the equation is \(Y=5-3X\), so the gradient is \(-3\).

blocks.html: Restore the original x and y after reading the parameters.

examples.title: Read a slope from a reciprocal model
examples.question: For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), \(y=\left(2+\frac6x\right)^3\). A graph uses \(X=\frac1x\). Choose \(Y\) so the graph is a straight line, and give its gradient and vertical intercept.
solution: Take the cube root of the whole relation to get \(\sqrt[3]{y}=2+\frac6x\). The reciprocal of \(x\) appears to the first power.
Set \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\) and replace \(\frac1x\) by \(X\). Then \(Y=6X+2\).
The gradient is \(6\) and the vertical intercept is \((0,2)\) on the extended straight line. \(X=0\) does not correspond to any finite positive \(x\).

examples.title: Identify what the slope means after squaring
examples.question: The positive variables satisfy \(y=\sqrt{9-\frac8x}\) on the part of the domain where the expression is defined. Use \(X=\frac1x\) to make a straight-line plot. State how the transformed output changes as \(X\) increases.
solution: Square the equation to get \(y^2=9-\frac8x\). The square removes the outer root.
With \(Y=y^2\), the equation becomes \(Y=9-8X\).
The transformed output decreases by \(8\) for every one-unit increase in \(X\). Positive \(y\) requires \(9-8X>0\).

examples.title: Turn a power into the gradient
examples.question: The model \(y=4x^3\) has \(x>0\). Use \(X=\log_2x\) to obtain a straight-line graph. Give its gradient and vertical intercept.
solution: Take base-2 logs. The product law gives \(\log_2y=\log_2 4+\log_2(x^3)\).
Now \(\log_2 4=2\), and by the power law \(\log_2(x^3)=3\log_2 x\). Thus \(Y=3X+2\) if \(Y=\log_2 y\).
The gradient is \(3\), and the vertical intercept is \((0,2)\). At \(x=1\), the original model gives \(y=4\), consistent with the intercept.

examples.title: Interpret a negative slope in a log–log graph
examples.question: A model has form \(y=Ax^n\), where \(A>0\) and \(x>0\). The graph of \(Y=\log_2y\) against \(X=\log_2x\) has gradient \(-2\) and vertical intercept \(3\). Find the original model and its value at \(x=4\).
solution: Taking base-2 logs gives \(Y=nX+\log_2 A\). The gradient is \(n=-2\), and the intercept gives \(\log_2 A=3\).
Undo the logarithm to obtain \(A=2^3=8\), so \(y=8x^{-2}\).
Substituting \(x=4\) gives \(y=\frac{8}{4^2}=\frac12\). A negative exponent makes the output decrease as \(x\) increases.

examples.title: Undo an exponential to straighten a graph
examples.question: For \(y=e^{2x^2+1}\), a plot uses \(X=x^2\). Choose a vertical coordinate giving a straight line and find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=1\).
solution: Take natural logarithms to remove the outer exponential. \(\ln y=2x^2+1\).
Now \(Y=\ln y\) gives \(Y=2X+1\). A plot of the original \(y\) against \(X\) would still be exponential.
At \(x=1\), \(X=1\), so \(Y=2(1)+1=3\). Return to the original output with \(y=e^Y=e^3\).

examples.title: Read the base of an exponential model
examples.question: For \(y=12\left(\frac12\right)^x\), transform the relation to a straight line using \(X=x\) and \(Y=\ln y\). State the gradient and vertical intercept.
solution: Use the product law of logarithms. \(\ln y=\ln12+\ln\left[\left(\frac12\right)^x\right]\).
Bring the exponent in front of the logarithm. \(Y=\ln12+x\ln\left(\frac12\right)\).
The gradient is \(\ln\left(\frac12\right)=-\ln 2\), and the vertical intercept is \(\ln12\). The negative gradient agrees with decay.

extraPractice.solution:
\(\log_2 y=\log_2 A+x\log_2 b\), so \(\log_2 b=-2\).

Therefore \(b=2^{-2}=\frac14\). The multiplier below 1 agrees with decay.

addmaths-0606-lines-recover-original-rel.description: Replace transformed variables and undo the corresponding operations in the right order.

sections.title: How do I undo squares and cubes?
sections.label: Powers
sections.intro: Read the transformed axes literally. A plot of y² against x³ does not give y directly.

blocks.html: If \(Y=y^2\) and \(X=x^3\), use \(y^2=ax^3+b\). Choose the square-root branch using the domain.

blocks.prompt:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=y^2\) against \(X=x^3\) has equation \(Y=11X+14\).

Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).
blocks.hint: Replace the transformed variables, then isolate y.
blocks.solution:
Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(y^2=11x^3+14\).

Take the positive square root because \(y>0\).

\(y=\sqrt{11x^3+14}\)

blocks.html: The root must cover the entire original expression for y².

blocks.prompt: A line has axes \(X=x^3\) and \(Y=y^2\), with \(Y=6X+1\). Given that \(y<0\), find \(y\) when \(x=2\).
blocks.hint: Find the value of \(Y\) first. Choose the root that gives the stated sign of \(y\).

retry.feedback: Both 7 and −7 square to 49. The stated branch requires a negative output.

blocks.html: If the question gives y positive, explain the branch you use.

sections.title: What happens when the vertical axis is exponential?
sections.label: Logs
sections.intro: Replace the axis name with the exponential. Then choose the appropriate logarithm.

blocks.html: From \(e^{2y}=ax^2+b\), take natural logs to get \(2y=\ln(ax^2+b)\) before dividing by two.

figure.alt: Three points on a straight line in transformed coordinates
figure.caption: The horizontal axis is X, the chosen expression in x. The vertical axis is Y, the chosen expression in y.

blocks.prompt:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=e^{2y}\) against \(X=x^2\) has equation \(Y=6X+17\).

Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).
blocks.hint: Replace the transformed variables, then isolate y.
blocks.solution:
Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(e^{2y}=6x^2+17\).

Take natural logs and then divide the resulting equation for \(2y\) by two.

\(y=\frac{1}{2}\ln(6x^2+17)\)

blocks.html: A factor in the exponent is still present after taking logs.

blocks.prompt: A transformed line is \(Y=3X+1\) with \(X=x^2\), \(Y=e^{2y}\) and \(x>0\). Find \(x\) when \(y=\ln 7\).
blocks.hint: Change \(y\) into \(Y\) before using the line. \(e^{2\ln7}=(e^{\ln7})^2\).

blocks.html: The argument of any logarithm must be positive.

sections.title: How do I undo mixed transformations?
sections.label: Cube root
sections.intro: Replace X and Y first. Focus on recovering the original output in the form requested.

blocks.html: If \(X=\ln x\) and \(Y=y^3\), then \(y=\sqrt[3]{a\ln x+b}\). When the model requires a positive output, require \(a\ln x+b>0\) as well as \(x>0\).

blocks.prompt:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=y^3\) against \(X=\ln x\) has equation \(Y=20X+2\).

Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).
blocks.hint: Replace the transformed variables, then isolate y.
blocks.solution:
Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(y^3=20\ln x+2\).

Take the cube root of the entire right side.

\(y=\sqrt[3]{20\ln x+2}\)

blocks.html: A cube root of a sum cannot be split into two cube roots.

blocks.title: Find the original inputs for a positive output
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), the graph of \(Y=y^3\) against \(X=\log_2x\) has equation \(Y=3X-6\). Find the set of original x-values for which \(y>0\).
blocks.hint: The cube root is positive exactly when \(3\log_2x-6>0\). Use the base 2 to convert back to \(x\).
blocks.solution: \(y>0\) requires \(\log_2 x>2\), so \(x>2^2=4\). At \(x=4\), \(y=0\), so the endpoint is excluded.

retry.feedback: The original output is zero at \(x=4\). The question requires a strictly positive output.

blocks.prompt: A line has axes \(Y=y^3\) and \(X=\ln x\), with \(Y=5X+8\). Find the original value of \(y\) at the transformed vertical intercept.
blocks.hint: On the transformed vertical axis, \(X=0\). Convert the resulting \(Y\) into \(y\).
blocks.solution: \(X=0\) gives \(Y=8\). Then \(y=\sqrt[3]{8}=2\). The original input is \(x=1\) because \(\ln1=0\).

blocks.html: Use the model only on the original domain supplied in the question.

examples.title: Recover the positive output from a squared axis
examples.question: On a graph of \(Y=y^2\) against \(X=x^3\), the line is \(Y=3X+1\). Given \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), find \(y\) in terms of \(x\) and find \(y\) at \(x=2\).
solution: Replace both transformed coordinates. \(y^2=3x^3+1\).
Since \(y>0\), take \(y=\sqrt{3x^3+1}\). The root applies to the whole right-hand side.

examples.title: Choose the square-root branch from the domain
examples.question: The graph has axes \(X=x^3\) and \(Y=y^2\), and its equation is \(Y=2X+9\). The original variables satisfy \(x\ge0\) and \(y<0\). Write \(y\) in terms of \(x\), and find \(y\) at \(x=2\).
solution: Replace the transformed variables to get \(y^2=2x^3+9\).
The radicand is positive for \(x\ge0\). On this domain, \(y<0\) selects \(y=-\sqrt{2x^3+9}\).

examples.title: Use a natural log to recover the output
examples.question: The axes are \(X=x^2\) and \(Y=e^{2y}\), and the transformed line is \(Y=3X+1\). Find \(y\) in terms of \(x\) and give its exact value at \(x=1\).
solution: Substitute the axis definitions to get \(e^{2y}=3x^2+1\). The expression on the right is positive for all real \(x\).
Take natural logs to obtain \(2y=\ln(3x^2+1)\). Dividing by \(2\) gives \(y=\frac12\ln(3x^2+1)\).

examples.title: Distinguish the two vertical intercepts
examples.question: A line has equation \(Y=5X+9\), with \(Y=e^{2y}\) and \(X=x^2\). The model includes \(x=0\). Give the vertical intercept in each set of coordinates.
solution: In transformed coordinates \(X=0\) gives \(Y=9\), so the intercept is \((0,9)\).
The original input is also \(x=0\), but the original output satisfies \(e^{2y}=9\). Hence \(y=\frac12\ln9=\ln3\).
The original graph intersects its vertical axis at \((0,\ln3)\). Recover each original coordinate using its own axis definition.

examples.title: Unpack a logarithmic input and a cubed output
examples.question: A graph of \(Y=y^3\) against \(X=\ln x\), with \(x>0\), has equation \(Y=5X+3\). Find \(y\) at \(x=e\) and give the original x-coordinate of the transformed vertical intercept.
solution: Replace the transformed coordinates to get \(y^3=5\ln x+3\), so \(y=\sqrt[3]{5\ln x+3}\).
The transformed vertical intercept has \(X=0\). Solve \(\ln x=0\) for the original input: \(x=e^0=1\).

examples.title: Recover a model and the inputs it can use
examples.question: Let \(x>0\) and \(y>0\). A graph of \(Y=y^3\) against \(X=\ln x\) has equation \(Y=2X-4\). Find \(y\) in terms of \(x\) and determine which \(x\)-values give \(y>0\).
solution: Substitute \(X=\ln x\) and \(Y=y^3\) to get \(y=\sqrt[3]{2\ln x-4}\).
A positive cube root requires \(2\ln x-4>0\), so \(\ln x>2\).
The natural logarithm increases with \(x\), so the model with \(y>0\) requires \(x>e^2\). At equality, the model gives \(y=0\).

examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy an unknown relation. The table shows points on the straight line obtained using \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\).

\(X\)\(Y\)
\(1\)\(19\)
\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(\frac{23}{2}\)
\(\frac{1}{3}\)\(9\)

  1. Find the gradient of the straight line.

    [2]

  2. Find an equation relating the original variables.

    [3]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=15\).

    [2]
solution: (a) Use the rows \((1,19)\) and \(\left(\frac13,9\right)\). The gradient is \(\frac{19-9}{1-\frac13}=\frac{10}{\frac23}=15\).
(b) At \(X=1\), \(19=15+c\), so \(c=4\). The model is \(\sqrt[3]{y}=4+\frac{15}{x}\).
Cube both sides to get \(y=\left(4+\frac{15}{x}\right)^3\). The third row is consistent with the same straight line.

examples.title: Use two transformed readings to predict a third
examples.question: The axes are \(X=\frac1x\) and \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\). The transformed line passes through \(\left(\frac12,7\right)\) and \(\left(\frac14,5\right)\). Find the original relation and predict \(y\) at \(x=8\).
solution: The gradient is \(\frac{7-5}{\frac12-\frac14}=8\). Substituting \(\left(\frac14,5\right)\) into \(Y=8X+c\) gives \(c=3\).
Restore the original variables. \(\sqrt[3]{y}=\frac8x+3\), so \(y=\left(\frac8x+3\right)^3\).
At \(x=8\) the transformed output is \(Y=4\). Cubing gives \(y=64\).

examples.title: Recover a growth model when the first input is not zero
examples.question: A model \(y=Ab^x\) with positive constants passes through \((1,10)\) and \((3,40)\). Find \(b\) and \(A\), then predict \(y\) when \(x=4\).
solution: From \(x=1\) to \(x=3\) there are two steps. Dividing \(Ab^3\) by \(Ab\) gives \(b^2=\frac{40}{10}=4\).
The base \(b\) is positive, so \(b=2\). Using \((1,10)\), \(10=A(2^1)\) gives \(A=5\).
The model is \(y=5(2^x)\). At \(x=4\), the predicted output is \(5(16)=80\).

examples.title: Recover the one-step multiplier of a decay model
examples.question: The readings \((2,64)\), \((5,8)\) and \((8,1)\) follow \(y=Ab^x\), with \(A>0\) and \(b>0\). Find \(b\), recover \(A\) and use the model to predict \(y\) at \(x=4\).
solution: The inputs 2 and 5 differ by 3. Taking the later output divided by the earlier output gives \(b^3=\frac8{64}=\frac18\), so \(b=\frac12\).
The data give \(64=A\left(\frac12\right)^2\), so \(A=256\).
The model gives \(y=256\left(\frac12\right)^4=16\) at \(x=4\). At \(x=8\), it also gives the observed value \(1\).

examples.question:
The table shows readings on a graph with axes \(X=x^2\) and \(Y=\ln y\) for \(x>0\) and \(y>0\).

\(X\)\(Y\)
\(1\)\(3\)
\(4\)\(6\)
\(9\)\(11\)

Find an equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\), then find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=\sqrt2\).
solution: Use \((1,3)\) and \((4,6)\). The gradient is \(\frac{6-3}{4-1}=1\). The next two rows give \(\frac{11-6}{9-4}=1\) as a check.
Substitute \((1,3)\) into \(Y=X+c\). Then \(3=1+c\), so \(c=2\).
Replace the transformed coordinates: \(\ln y=x^2+2\). Undo the log to obtain \(y=e^{x^2+2}\).
At \(x=\sqrt2\), \(X=2\), so \(Y=4\) and \(y=e^4\). This is interpolation because \(X=2\) is between two measured values.

examples.question: The straight-line model is \(Y=2X+3\), where \(X=x^2\), \(Y=\ln y\), \(x>0\) and \(y>0\). Find the original input when \(y=e^{21}\).
solution: The target \(y=e^{21}\) gives \(Y=21\). Solve \(21=2X+3\) to get \(X=9\).
Because \(X=x^2\) and \(x>0\), the original input is \(\sqrt9=3\).
Substitution gives \(\ln y=2(3^2)+3=21\), as required.
